newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian gasoline heads outside region amid glut.
newsitem.headline: Asian gasoline heads outside region amid glut.

text.p: Asian gasoline is increasingly being exported to Europe, Africa and the United States as refiners and traders seek new markets for the region's surplus supplies, industry sources said on Tuesday.
Traditionally, little gasoline has been exported outside Asia, partly because of price factors but also because of different quality specifications.
Until recently only a few such shipments were made each year. But several new refineries have opened in Asia, especially in South Korea and Thailand, at a time when demand is stagnant.
"There is a great incentive for majors and traders to move the barrels outside the region as demand is in the doldrums," said one trader.
Already, players have put together cargoes for export in September to Africa and the West, the sources said.
But exporting gasoline from Asia to Europe or the United States is "more complicated than a simple matter for the arbitrage to open", one trader said.
Gasoline produced in Thailand and South Korea for export is usually about 92-octane. In Europe or the United States, buyers want 95-octane.
Nor does Asian gasoline contain oxygenates such as methyl tertiary butyl ether (MTBE), which is used to boost octane values and make gasoline burn cleaner.
"These things cost money and as a result it is not easy to move cargoes to the West or the U.S.," the trader said.
But the recent substantial decline in Asian prices and the more important glut of supplies has forced players to look to market their gasoline further afield.
Benchmark Singapore prices have tumbled US$6.00 per barrel in the past four months and stood at $21.50 on Monday.

One source said deals have been struck to export one 250,000-barrel cargo each to Africa and the West for shipment at the end of August or early September after blending in Singapore to meet stringent specifications.
The source declined to elaborate on the deal, but said it was rare for gasoline to be exported from Singapore to the West.
The Asian supply glut came to a head in July when Thailand started to offer several prompt spot cargoes for export when its new refineries started operating at full capacity.
Thailand opened the 145,000 barrel per day (bpd) Rayong and the 130,000 bpd Star Petroleum refineries this year, forcing another Thai refiner, Thai Oil, to offer products for export.

Traders said they estimated Thailand would export about 1.3 million barrels of gasoline a month. Gasoline from Thailand is already being used by blenders for sales to Taiwan and is being exported to Australia.

The opening of the Australian market to independent wholesalers led to the building of two storage terminals. Their operators, Mitsui & Co Ltd and Wickland Terminals Asia Ltd, have bought some of their requirements from Thailand, traders said.
This, in turn, has turned Australia into an exporter as refiners there grappled with excess supplies.

Early last week, Australia's Ampol Petroleum Pty Ltd sold a 30,000-tonne 92-octane cargo to U.S. refiner Koch Oil. Trade sources said Koch planned to take the cargo to the United States -- the first time Australian gasoline has been shipped there.

South Korea is also producing gasoline for export. One refiner said South Korean refiners were offering reformate and low octane gasoline for export, mainly sold to blenders for resale to Taiwan or even the United States.
